title: Rick's Car Battery Is Powered by an Entire Universe

cuts.voiceover_text: Rick and Morty are inside Rick's battered spaceship, staring at a failing power system. Rick spots the problem: the pipe should be sending twenty terawatts to the engine, but it is sending zero. Morty looks through the window and sees an entire civilization below them. The repair job just became a field trip.

Rick explains what he built. He trapped a void in a temporal field, waited for a planet to develop intelligent life, then taught its people about electricity. Their civilization now generates power on a global scale, and Rick siphons some of it to run his engine and charge his phone. Morty stares at the tiny world in disbelief. Rick calls it society. Morty calls it slavery with extra steps.

Rick meets Zeep, the brilliant scientist who has replaced the planet's old Google boxes with something even more ambitious. Zeep reveals a container holding an infinite universe, complete with a planet capable of generating massive power. He calls it a miniverse. Rick and Morty enter the machine and watch the miniature civilization below. Zeep has taught its people to make electricity with flubble cranks, while secretly routing eighty percent of that energy back to his own world. His battery is a battery inside Rick's battery.

Morty sees the workers turning the cranks and finally says what everyone is thinking. Zeep is harvesting their labor to power his own world. Zeep insists they are paid, housed, and allowed to form families, but Morty is not buying the rebrand. Slavery with extra steps. Rick initially mocks him, then Morty points out the obvious hypocrisy: Rick is doing the exact same thing. Rick's grand plan is to make Zeep discover microverse technology, realize he is a hypocrite, and go back to the old system. Somehow, ice cream is still part of the strategy.

Rick pretends to offer the tiny civilization more alien technology, then casually asks whether any scientist is building a universe in a box. The president freezes. That secret project already exists. Rick follows the clue to another lab, where a white scientist demonstrates his own miniature universe. He plans to accelerate time, wait for intelligent life, and introduce it to electricity through a pulley device. The new scientist understands the arrangement immediately: most of the energy will be taken from the people inside.

The new scientist calls the plan wrong. Rick's answer is painfully familiar. The people will work for each other, exchange money, and somehow that makes everything fine. Morty delivers the same verdict again: slavery with extra steps. Then Rick stops mid-argument. If this scientist made a universe, and Zeep made the one above it, Rick finally knows what his own battery contains.

Rick looks from Zeep to the white scientist and sees the nesting pattern. Every genius has built a universe for the genius above him. Morty watches the explanation unfold while the scientists argue over who created whom. The battery is not one universe. It is a stack of them.

Rick threatens to smash the teenyverse, then escape through the surrounding miniverse and finally the microverse around that. Morty warns him not to make things worse, but Rick points out the practical problem: they need the universe inside his battery to start the car. Zeep fires back that Rick used his world for exactly the same reason. Rick refuses to feel guilty and starts crafting a way out. The argument ends where it began: every universe is powering something above it.
